sketches.title: Room for Improvement
sketches.premise: You are writing a safety announcement for an ordinary room, but your announcement has one important job: it must make the room sound safer without pretending it is a different room. Both players answer the same card, and the host awards points for how much useful, vivid safety advice you add while staying in the room.
sketches.criterion: The announcement must keep the named room and its everyday purpose true while turning the two named objects into a sensible safety warning.
sketches.move_shape: Write one cheerful announcement of up to 160 characters using both objects and the room; for example, for a bedroom with a lamp and a rug: "Keep the lamp steady and the rug flat, so bedtime stays cozy instead of becoming a surprise floor trip."

sketches.title: Mind the Gap
sketches.premise: A normal room has two harmless objects, and one small gap, edge, or loose bit is waiting to cause trouble. Write the safety announcement that spots the danger most clearly while remaining completely believable for that room; the host rewards detail, not drama.
sketches.criterion: The move must identify a plausible safety risk involving both named objects in the named room, without changing what either object is or what the room is for.
sketches.move_shape: Write one safety notice of up to 160 characters; for example, for a hallway with a shoe and a mat: "Keep shoes off the mat’s edge, where a hurried foot could catch and send the hallway into an unwanted cartwheel."

sketches.title: Please Stay Put
sketches.premise: The host announces two everyday things in a room, and you give them a gentle instruction to stay safely where they belong. Your sentence earns more points when the instruction is precise, useful, and pleasantly surprising, but it must still sound like something a real safety sign could say.
sketches.criterion: The move must give both named objects a physically possible safety instruction that fits their normal use in the named room.
sketches.move_shape: Write one safety announcement of up to 160 characters; for example, for a classroom with a chair and a backpack: "Chairs stay under desks, and backpacks stay out of the aisle, because feet deserve a clear route to learning."

sketches.title: The Kind of Caution
sketches.premise: Every card names a normal room and two ordinary objects. Write a warm warning that connects them through one cause-and-effect chain, as if a caring adult is helping everyone notice a tiny problem before it becomes a big one.
sketches.criterion: The move must show a believable cause-and-effect safety chain in which both named objects matter and the room remains an ordinary room.
sketches.move_shape: Write one sentence of up to 160 characters; for example, for a garage with a box and a broom: "Stack the box securely and park the broom upright, so one wobble does not turn tidying into a domino show."

sketches.title: Exit With Care
sketches.premise: The room is normal, the objects are ordinary, and someone is about to move through it. Make a safety announcement that helps that person enter, cross, or leave without giving away the room’s hidden real-world fact; the best move is helpful and hard to predict.
sketches.criterion: The move must give safe movement advice that uses both named objects and keeps the room’s concealed checkable fact undisclosed.
sketches.move_shape: Write one announcement of up to 160 characters; for example, for an entryway with an umbrella and a door: "Check the umbrella is tucked away before opening the door, so the next arrival gets a welcome rather than a poke."

sketches.title: Nothing to See but Safety
sketches.premise: The host reads a room, two objects, and a safety announcement with one missing fact. You must make the announcement sound complete without stating that hidden fact, while the host gives more points for elegant clues than for loud alarms.
sketches.criterion: The move must be a useful safety announcement involving both objects that leaves the card’s concealed true detail unstated.
sketches.move_shape: Write one sentence of up to 160 characters; for example, for a kitchen with a window and a curtain: "Keep the curtain clear of the window’s working parts, so fresh air can arrive without bringing the fabric along."
